1:
Ellicott takes the discourse as placed at the forefront of this Gospel for a reason, a pattern sermon representing the teaching with which the work began, quoted in the first age of the church oftener than any other part. Whether it is one discourse he treats as a real question, since much of it recurs scattered through Luke, where the same sayings come as answers to questions or rebukes of particular faults. Against that he sets the evidence of a systematic plan: the conditions of blessedness first, then the contrast between the righteousness of the kingdom and that current among the scribes, carried through their handling of the commandments and through almsgiving, prayer and fasting. He concludes for substantially a single discourse.

Whether Luke reports the same sermon is disputed. Ellicott holds the two quite distinct. Calvin calls the opinion that they differ light and frivolous, resting on nothing but the mountain in the one and the plain in the other, a mistake about how Luke's words connect; the design of both was to collect the leading points of Christ's doctrine into one place. Robertson finds no real difficulty in taking them as one, and reconciles the settings from Luke's own account, that after a night of prayer and the choice of the twelve he came down to a level place on the mountain. Barnes leaves it open, thinking the substance not improbably repeated on different occasions and to different people, with parts omitted, Luke recording one of those.

Why he went up is answered variously. Clarke supposes nothing more than a small hill, since on a high mountain he could not have been heard and at a distance he would not have sat down; he went up for the advantage of speaking. Barnes agrees that an eminence was more convenient, and notes the hill tradition marks as the Mount of Beatitudes, while allowing there is no positive evidence for it. Robertson insists on the article, the mountain and not a mountain, and has him go up to get into closer contact with the disciples. Calvin dismisses the allegory that the ascent was to teach them to lift their minds above worldly employments: the design was a retreat away from the crowd. Henry makes the mountain part of the lesson, a common mountain and not one of the holy mountains, there being no such distinguishing holiness of places now, and sets the scene against Sinai: then the Lord came down upon the mountain, now he went up; then he spoke in thunder and lightning, now in a still small voice; then the people were ordered to keep their distance, now they are invited to draw near.

The sitting and the opening of the mouth are read in the same two ways. Clarke calls sitting the usual posture of public teachers among the Jews, so much so that it became a word for teaching; Henry makes it a set sermon rather than an occasional one, delivered with the sedateness of a lawgiver, and takes the opening of the mouth for a Hebrew periphrasis of speaking. Calvin calls the phrase a redundancy after the Hebrew idiom and prefers that to the emphatic account. Wesley holds that it always denotes a set and solemn discourse, and reads the whole as the complete art of happiness, taught by one who lays aside the lofty style of command to insinuate his will more gently. Robertson hears volume in it. All agree the hearers were more than the twelve: Clarke glosses the word as scholar, those who put themselves under his tuition; Barnes warns that learners does not mean they were all Christians; Wesley takes in all who desired to learn; and Henry observes that the speech was directed to the disciples, who followed for love and learning while others attended only for cures, but spoken in the hearing of the multitude.
3:
Henry notes that the sermon begins with blessings, the Old Testament having ended with a curse, and that they come first to prepare the hearers rather than last to dismiss them. The design is to rectify the ruinous mistake of a carnal world, whose opinion is that the rich and great are the happy, and to remove the discouragements of the poor, since even the least in the kingdom whose heart is upright is happy in its honours. Clarke finds the same in the word, deriving happy from a root meaning not subject to fate, so that the man Christ calls happy is governed not by chance but by an all-wise providence. Wesley reads the eight as a sweet invitation to holiness, annexed to so many steps in Christianity.

What the poverty is divides them. Gill rules out the poor in purse, since God has called many in that condition but not all. Ellicott says the qualifying clause points to the region of life in which the poverty is found, and that Luke, lacking it, speaks of outward poverty as a less perilous state than riches. Henry defines it as being emptied of self in order to be filled with Christ, and notes that the philosophers did not reckon humility among the virtues at all. Calvin dissents: since Luke and Matthew must mean the same thing, the name belongs to those pressed and afflicted by adversity, the added epithet confining the happiness to those who under the discipline of the cross have learned to be humble. He reads the hunger and thirst the same way, as a figure for suffering want and being defrauded of one's right, where Henry allows that reading of oppressed men denied justice but holds the spiritual sense certain, and Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott take the craving for righteousness alone.

On meekness Barnes insists it is neither meanness nor cowardice nor a surrender of rights but patience in receiving injuries, and cites Christ before the officer who struck him and Paul standing on his citizenship. Clarke derives the word from a root meaning easy, and notes that our gentleman once carried the sense. Calvin admits the promise looks foolish, since the ready avengers are the men who seem to claim the earth, and answers with the diabolical proverb that we must howl with the wolves; Henry calls the inheritance almost the only express temporal promise in the New Testament. Clarke takes mercy in its fullest latitude, both the pardon of injuries and almsgiving, tracing the Latin word to pain of heart; Gill divides it between the bodies and souls of men. Ellicott notes that the peacemaker's beatitude rightly follows the pure in heart, since it is the absence of all baseness that gives power to make peace.

The persecution clause they treat as the hardest. Ellicott finds three forms of suffering in it, the vague contempt of nicknames, persecution generally, and deliberate calumnies such as the charges of foul banquets spread against early believers; and he reports that falsely is absent from the best manuscripts, probably added to guard against a man claiming the reward while really guilty. Clarke, taking the verb for a forensic term covering legal accusation, remembers the numbers burnt alive under Queen Mary. Barnes warns that we are not to seek persecution or provoke it by strange conduct, yet notes that many early Christians threw themselves in the way of their persecutors. Calvin says we cannot be Christ's soldiers on any other condition than that the greater part of the world rise against us, and refutes the reasonings about the word reward, there being no mutual relation between reward and merit; Ellicott agrees it is not of debt but of grace. Henry observes that this beatitude is doubled, like Pharaoh's dream, because it is hardly credited, and that it is not the suffering but the cause that makes the martyr.
13:
Whether salt can really lose its savour is the first question. Barnes says the salt of his own country is a compound in which saltness enters into the nature of the substance, so that if it went nothing would remain; but eastern salt was impure, mingled with earthy matter, and might lose all its saltness and leave the earth behind. Clarke settles it from a traveller's report of the Valley of Salt, where a piece broken from the precipice had lost its savour where rain, sun and air reached it, the inner part next the rock retaining it. Ellicott reports the same traveller and the rock-salt from the Dead Sea shore known as the Salt of Sodom, but adds that he knows of no recent confirmation. Robertson answers from observation, that in Syria and Palestine one sees salt in piles on the ground because it has lost its flavour, the most worthless thing imaginable, and suspects a current proverb.

Who is addressed is the second. Calvin takes it of the apostles and now of the pastors of the church, to whom the designation belongs in a peculiar manner, and presses the threat in it: corruption tolerable in others would in them be monstrous, and where are they to find the remedy they are themselves supposed to supply? Gill reads it of the apostles, salt for their savoury doctrine and savoury lives alike, and of the whole earth and not Judea only. Henry agrees that Christians, and especially ministers, are the salt of the earth, and infers that they must not be laid in a heap but scattered as salt upon meat, as the Levites were dispersed in Israel. Barnes extends it to ministers and to all Christians. Ellicott takes the disciples in their ideal character, the germ of a new Israel called to a prophetic work, and hears the sacrificial use of salt behind the words as well as the antiseptic one.

On the light Clarke observes that light of the world was a title given to the most eminent rabbis, which Christ takes from them and gives to his disciples, and Gill says the same of what the Jews claimed for their council and doctors. Ellicott insists the word belongs in its truest sense to Christ alone, the lamp of the next verse showing that even here the disciples shine with a derived brightness. For the city Ellicott suggests Safed, high above the sea and commanding one of the grandest views in Palestine, perhaps in sight; Henry turns the figure on the gospel itself, carrying so much of its own evidence that it cannot be hid from any who do not wilfully shut their eyes.

The lamp and the measure are read from the cottage. Robertson describes the single room with its projecting stone for the lamp, the one earthenware grain measure, and the stand, a lamp-stand throughout and not a candlestick; Ellicott notes that the definite article implies familiarity, each cottage having one such article, and that the lamp was the cheap portable vessel of the poor. Clarke reports from ancient writers that only those with bad designs hid a light under a measure, to rise in the night with it ready for murder. All of them meet the objection that good works are afterwards to be hidden: Calvin answers that the later command forbids ostentation only, while here the object is the glory of God alone, and that if good works are not traced to God it is an open insult to extol free will; Barnes says it is not right to do a thing merely to be seen, for that is pride, but that being seen God may be honoured; Ellicott calls the motive the direct opposite of the Pharisee's; and Henry, that we must do good works that may be seen to the edification of others, not to our own ostentation.
17:
Ellicott marks a new section here, running to the end of the chapter: the discourse turns against the current teaching of the scribes, which sometimes held the letter and neglected the spirit and sometimes overrode even the letter by unauthorised traditions. The words think not, he adds, imply that men had begun so to think. Lightfoot supplies the expectation behind it, that the nation looked for a Messiah who would advance the Mosaic law to its highest pitch, so the scribes objected that this could not be he, since he abolished the traditions they obtruded in place of Moses; the answer is that he abolished not the law when he abolished the traditions.

What fulfil means is drawn out variously. Henry takes it in five senses: to obey the commands, never breaking them; to make good its promises and the predictions that bore witness to him; to answer its types, making good rather than making void the ceremonial law; to fill up its defects, as water poured into a vessel not to empty it but to fill it to the brim, or a picture first rough-drawn and afterwards filled up; and to carry on the same design, the gospel being not the repeal of the law but its amendment. Clarke reads the word as complete, the law being in itself only the shadow of good things to come, to which Christ added what was needed to perfect it, his own sacrifice, without which it could neither satisfy God nor sanctify men. Wesley has him establish, illustrate and explain its highest meaning by his life and doctrine.

Barnes identifies the yod as the smallest Hebrew letter and the tittle as the points that distinguish one letter from another, a change in which might alter a word, so that the Jews would destroy a whole manuscript for the smallest slip. Lightfoot shows the traditional doctors using the same seal as the asseveration here, saying they speak in truth, and that wherever this is said it is a tradition of Moses from Sinai, against whose insolence Christ sets his own oracles. Till all be fulfilled is read two ways. Calvin refuses the refinement that the day of judgment will end the law, declining to feed his readers' ears with such amusements, and insists the words refer not to the life of men, since even the regenerate keep the law imperfectly, but to the perfect truth of the doctrine. Wesley gives it the other turn, that the law has its effect when rewards are given and punishments inflicted as well as when its precepts are obeyed.

The least commandments are disputed too. Ellicott denies that the ceremonial law is meant, since the usage of the time confined the word to moral laws and the context deals with nothing else, and takes the least to be those that seemed trivial yet were really great, the control of thoughts and desires and words against the greater commands about acts. Calvin says expressly the ten words, and calls the epithet least a concession to men's judgment, since nothing from that sacred mouth may be thought little. Barnes and Clarke trace the distinction to the Pharisees, who divided the precepts into greater and lesser and made violating the lesser a trivial offence, Clarke comparing the distinction of mortal and venial sins. What is charged against them at the last Calvin weighs carefully: most commentators take it of their lives, but he asks whether the corrupted manner of teaching is not rather in view, since by confining the law to outward duties they trained their disciples like apes to hypocrisy, and he is willing to include both. Henry grants them what is due, that they were much in fasting and prayer and almsgiving and punctual in the ceremonial appointments, and concludes that the religion Christ establishes does not only exclude their badness but excels their goodness.
21:
Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering, said to them of old time, and takes the impersonal form and the tone of authority as conclusive against referring the quoted words to the Law as God gave it through Moses. Lightfoot reads heard as received by tradition and says the words quoted carry the false paint of tradition; Christ names those of old because the memory of the ancient fathers of the traditions was venerable. Calvin denies flatly that this is a correction or an enlargement of the law: the prevailing opinion, that the beginning of righteousness was laid down in the ancient law and its perfection in the Gospel, was farthest of all from Christ's design. Henry says the same, that he adds nothing new but limits abused permissions.

Whether the words without a cause belong to the text divides them sharply. Clarke reports them wanting in the Vatican manuscript and in many versions and fathers, judges them a marginal gloss that crept in, and would render the Greek vainly instead. Ellicott leaves it open: they are absent from many of the best copies and may have been inserted to soften a harsh teaching, or may have stood there first and been struck out as giving too wide a margin for excuses. Wesley argues from the scope of the discourse, that the clause is utterly foreign to it: if only causeless anger were forbidden there was no need of so solemn a declaration, the scribes having taught that much, and this righteousness would not exceed theirs. Henry and Barnes both build on the clause as genuine: Henry glosses it as without just provocation, without good end, and beyond due bounds, and Barnes distinguishes the anger that is lawful, since God is angry with the wicked and Christ looked on the Pharisees with anger.

At the altar Ellicott makes the moment one for self-scrutiny, the question being not whether he has a complaint but whether any has cause of complaint against him; he cites the rule that a man who remembers leaven left in the house should return and remove it before finishing the Passover, the leaven of bread yielding here to the leaven of malice. Lightfoot shows the Jewish teachers restraining the duty to pecuniary damages and bare restitution, which might be done without a charitable mind, where Christ extends it to every offence. Calvin meets the objection that charity would then outrank the worship of God: the words mean only that it is a false and empty profession which is made by men who deal unjustly with their brethren.

On the adversary they divide again. Clarke calls the word a perfect law term, the plaintiff, and takes the counsel as legal prudence, a suit being costly and the winner gaining nothing in the end; but he warns that those who make the adversary God, the judge Christ, the officer Death and the prison Hell abuse the passage and highly dishonour God. Barnes agrees there is no propriety in regarding God as the sinner's adversary here, though the imprisonment is court language for dealings real enough. Ellicott divides it, the judge being God and the officers those who execute his judgment, while the adversary is the neighbour we have wronged; the whole teaching, he observes, is addressed to one who has done wrong. Henry takes the step Clarke and Barnes refuse, making the great God a law-adversary who has an action against sinners. Calvin turns it another way again, as spoken to take away occasion for hatred by reproving the obstinacy of men too tenacious of their own rights. Whether the last farthing can ever be paid Ellicott asks without answering; Clarke says unwarrantable violence must be used before the text will serve either purgatory or universal restoration; and Henry with Wesley holds it never paid, since divine justice will be for ever in the satisfying but never satisfied.
27:
Lightfoot shows what the gloss had done: the old teachers interpreted the commandment of the act only, and of the act with a married woman. Henry presses the wider sense, that the looking is not upon another man's wife only, as some would have it, but upon any woman. Calvin calls the mention of the eye a part put for the whole, since not the eyes only but the concealed flames of the heart make a man an adulterer, lust entering as it were by that door. Ellicott marks the force of the Greek, that it is not the passing glance nor even the momentary impulse but the continued gaze by which it is deliberately cherished into a passion;, and refuses to let the parallels in Seneca and Epictetus disparage it, since the light that lightens every man has led others to the same truth.

The eye and the hand raise two further questions. On the word rendered offend Ellicott prefers the Geneva version's cause thee to offend, the verb meaning to make another stumble into a snare; Robertson sharpens it, the noun being the stick in the trap that closes it when the animal touches it. Whether the plucking out is to be taken literally they divide. Ellicott says the bold severity of the phrase excludes a literal reading, since the evil is seated in the will and not the organ, so that removing the instrument might leave the inward taint unpurified. Calvin calls it an exaggerated form of speech, Christ not meaning that we must mutilate the body but that whatever hinders obedience must be cut off. Robertson agrees the vivid pictures plead for self-mastery, not mutilation. Clarke pushes the other way: it is not enough to shut the eye or stop the hand, the one must be plucked out and the other cut off, and we must cast them both from us. Henry allows the severity but adds, in a parenthesis, that by grace there is another way.

On divorce they agree about the practice and differ about the remedy. Ellicott sets out the two schools: Shammai held the uncleanness of the precept to mean unchastity only, while Hillel held, as Milton did among Christian teachers, that anything making the wife's company distasteful was ground enough. Clarke supplies the instances, the saying attributed to Akiba that a man who saw a woman handsomer than his wife might put her away, and the historian's cool notice that he put away the wife who had borne him three children, not being pleased with her manners. Barnes puts it plainly, that whatever the schools said, the husband was judge in his own case and dismissed his wife when and for what cause he chose.

What the exception allows is disputed. Clarke objects to the rendering fornication, which properly means the connection of unmarried persons, and would translate on account of whoredom; a Christian, he adds, ought rather to beg grace to bear his wife's imperfections than to think of parting from her. Ellicott takes the generic term as chosen to include sin before marriage as well as after, and reads the clause as asserting that where divorce is got on any other ground, man's law, even that of Moses, stands at variance with the eternal law of God. Lightfoot distinguishes: Christ does not abrogate the Mosaic permission but tolerates it inside the Mosaic bounds, and even in the case of adultery imposes no compulsion but indulges a liberty, where the Jewish courts had sometimes whipped a man into putting his wife away. Robertson notes the objection that the exception cannot be Christ's own, since Mark and Luke omit it and the early Christians may have added it, and answers that this looks like criticism framed for modern needs. Calvin says that such a husband, abandoning the wife God gave him, is justly condemned for having prostituted her to others.
33:
Lightfoot states the fault of the old teaching exactly: the fathers of the traditions reduced the whole sin of swearing to perjury and cared little for a rash oath, troubling themselves scarcely at all with how often a man swore, so long as what he swore was true. Ellicott adds the second half of the mischief, that they allowed many forms of oath in which the holy name was not uttered, as though to guard it from desecration, and then counted some binding and others not, tampering with men's sense of truthfulness by a casuistry at once subtle, irrational and dishonest.

Whether swear not at all forbids every oath is the great question. Ellicott grants that the first impression favours those who think so, naming the Society of Friends, and holds that such scruples deserve tender dealing; but he judges the conclusion mistaken on three grounds, that Christ would then be repealing part of the moral law and destroying rather than fulfilling it, that he himself answered a solemn adjuration when he had before been silent and Paul repeatedly used such forms of attestation, and that the context is against it. Calvin is less patient: many have been led by the phrase into the false notion that every kind of swearing is condemned, and the Anabaptists have blustered on it, but the enumerated kinds were added by way of exposition, so that the words relate not to the substance but to the form and mean neither directly nor indirectly; to press a single word while passing over the whole scope betrays not only a rage for controversy but gross ignorance. Lightfoot finds the middle way, that the sense goes between the Jew, who allowed some place for an arbitrary oath, and the Anabaptist, who allows none for a necessary one. Henry agrees that swearing rightly done is a part of religious worship, and makes the magistrate the judge of the necessity: we may be sworn, but we must not swear.

The particular forms are read alike. Henry shows that there is nothing we can swear by which is not some way related to God, so that it is as dangerous to swear by the creature as by him: heaven is his throne, the earth his footstool, Jerusalem the city of the great King, and the head more God's than ours, since we cannot change the colour of one hair. Barnes adds that oaths by inanimate objects are either unmeaning or are oaths by the living Being who has power to take vengeance, and that to swear by the head is to swear by the life, which is not ours to pledge.

On the remedy they agree and then divide over its last clause. Gill, who holds that the words are not to be taken in the strictest sense, observes that the Jews have no reason to reject the counsel, since they themselves praise their doctors by saying that their words in doctrine and in dealing are yea, yea. Clarke seals it from Homer, that the man whose words agree not with his thoughts is as detestable as the gates of hell. Calvin finds the cause of much swearing in the lying and unsteadiness that leave men not knowing whom to trust, and rejects the exposition charging the guilt on the man who will not credit another's word, holding rather that men's own wickedness compels them to swear. What cometh of evil means is left open. Ellicott, with some hesitation, takes the Greek as masculine, these fantastic oaths coming not from him who is the Truth but from him who speaks a lie of his own; Clarke reports a manuscript and a fourth-century commentator reading of the devil outright; Henry gives both, an ancient copy reading from the evil one, and the thing itself coming from the corruption of men's nature and the deceitfulness that makes men distrust each other.
38:
All of them read the old rule as judicial. Ellicott calls it in essence a limit in both directions, a check on the wild justice of revenge: not less than eye for eye, which might lead to connivance in guilt, and not more, which would open a fresh score of wrong; the scribes made it a rule of private retaliation and so the sanction of a temper that forgives nothing. Barnes says that as a judicial rule it is not unjust and that Christ finds no fault with it as applied to magistrates, the Jews having extended to private conduct what was given only to regulate the bench.

What is not to be resisted, and how far, divides them. Clarke is fully persuaded the Greek means the evil person, and reads the sense as do not repel one outrage by another. Ellicott finds the word able to be masculine or neuter and prefers the masculine, not the evil one of pre-eminence but the human evil-doer, remarking that of the mightier evil one we are expressly told it is our duty to resist him. On the letter of the precept Ellicott puts the question directly, whether the words were meant to be obeyed literally, observing that most men feel they cannot act on them so, and that the attempt would throw society into confusion and make the meek the victims. Robertson answers that the language is bold and picturesque and not to be pressed, and that what is certainly meant is that personal revenge is taken out of our hands; he allows defence against robbery and murder, and adds that professional pacifism may be mere cowardice. Henry guards the same ground, that the precept does not repeal the law of self-preservation or the care we owe our families, and Barnes that Christ did not mean we should see our families murdered rather than resist. Calvin distinguishes two ways of resisting, by warding off injury through inoffensive conduct and by retaliation, and says only the second is forbidden.

The two garments are disputed. Ellicott makes the coat the close-fitting tunic worn next the body and the cloke the outer flowing mantle, the more costly of the two; Robertson agrees, the coat being a sort of shirt that would be demanded at law while a robber would seize the outer garment first. Clarke reverses them, the coat being the upper garment and the cloke the under, what we call the strait coat and the great coat; and Lightfoot supports him from the Talmud, the word being the talith, so called because it is above all the garments. Calvin keeps the precept from absurdity: none but a fool would make it mean that we must yield what is demanded before coming into court, which would only inflame the greedy, and Christians are not wholly forbidden lawsuits where they have a just defence.

On the compelling they agree. Barnes, Ellicott, Clarke and Robertson all trace the word to the Persian couriers stationed along the royal roads, who might press horses, boats and men for the king's despatches, and Robertson notes that the same verb is used of Simon of Cyrene compelled to carry the cross. On the giving Ellicott finds another paradox, a principle binding upon every one put in the form of a rule whose letter binds no man, since to give all men what they ask would often be to curse rather than bless them; Calvin says Christ meant to make his disciples generous and not prodigal, demanding a beneficence that looks for no return; Barnes draws the practical limits, that it is seldom good to give to a man able to work, though a widow or an orphan should never be sent away empty; and Clarke asks that if we will not relieve a poor man we at least never give him an ill word nor an ill look.
43:
Wesley puts it in a line: God spoke the former part and the scribes added the latter. Barnes calls the hatred an inference the Jews drew, supposing that to love the one they must hate the other, strangers to the law that requires us to love both. Calvin thinks it astonishing that they fell into so great an absurdity as to limit the word to benevolent persons, since in speaking of our neighbours God includes the whole human race. Henry holds the gloss flatly against the Law, which forbade them to abhor an Edomite or an Egyptian, and reads the commission against the devoted nations as a particular case to make room for Israel. Ellicott will not go so far: as to national enemies the words can hardly be called foreign to the spirit of the Law, since Israel was practically commanded to hate the nations it was sent to destroy; the fault of the scribes was to stereotype a law transitory in its nature and then extend it to private enmities.

What the love is they define carefully. Barnes separates two loves springing from the same goodwill, complacency in another's conduct and benevolence towards his person, and it is the second we owe our enemies: we may hate the conduct of a man who reviles us and still wish him well, pity his folly and speak kindly of him. Clarke calls the precept the most sublime piece of morality ever given to man, and reasonable rather than absurd, since he who hates another is necessarily miserable; no false religion imposes a yoke so contrary to self-love, and none but he who has the mind of Christ can keep it. Ellicott marks the stress laid on prayer as the highest utterance of that love, since circumstances may preclude acts that would be rejected and words met with scorn, while the prayer that they too may be delivered is always in our power.

On the publicans Lightfoot cites the canons that trained the nation in hatred, not of the Gentiles only but of Israelites who would not walk in the same traditions, and the rulings that joined publicans with robbers. Ellicott observes that our Lord puts himself for the moment on the level of his hearers, speaking their familiar language with a widely different application: were they after all above the publicans, if they confined their love to a reciprocity of good offices? Wesley turns the salutation on the church, guessing that the glance is at the prejudices of rival sects, and wishing it had been better attended to among the unhappy divisions into which the church has been crumbled.

What perfect means divides them along confessional lines. Barnes takes the word in its mechanical sense, of a thing complete in its parts, and instances Job, called perfect though fault is afterwards found with him, his piety being proportionate and consistent throughout. Ellicott reads the Greek as an ideal future that implies an imperative, the perfection being the attainment of the end of our being. Calvin denies any equality of measure: the word relates solely to resemblance, and the perfection of God here means that free and pure kindness which is not induced by expectation of gain and which contends with the malice and ingratitude of men. Clarke takes the words as command and promise together, and answers the question whether we can be fully saved from sin in this world by saying that as in the infinite nature there is nothing but goodness, so in our finite nature no sin shall dwell. Wesley reads it the same way, that the holiness described in the chapter is recommended at the beginning as happiness and sealed at the close as perfection, and that knowing how ready our unbelief would be to cry that this is impossible, he stakes on it all the faithfulness of him to whom all things are possible.
